hypothesis: An adversary who compromised Windows hosts in this network stole credentials from them (MITRE ATT&CK tactic: Credential Access).

frame.restated: An adversary with existing access to Windows hosts on this network is stealing credentials from those hosts.
frame.what_would_confirm: Observable evidence such as LSASS process memory access (e.g., via Mimikatz or procdump), suspicious access to SAM/SECURITY registry hives, use of Windows Credential Manager APIs, or anomalous authentication events indicating credential theft.
frame.what_would_refute: Absence of any credential dumping tool execution, no unauthorized access to LSASS or registry hives, and no anomalous credential-related events on the compromised Windows hosts.

verdict.rule: Confirmed if >=1 in-scope incident of verified malicious findings (confidence >= medium); Inconclusive if only suspicious incidents or coverage gaps; Refuted if full coverage and no malicious/suspicious finding

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: LSASS memory was accessed with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS by PowerShell.exe on scranton, consistent with OS credential dumping.

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF on scranton at 03:05:16; wsmprovhost.exe opened lsass with 0x1F3FFF on nashua at 03:09:29.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: lsass.exe wrote HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F on scranton, but by the legitimate hive owner; no external hive copy observed.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No NTDS.dit access, vssadmin/diskshadow/ntdsutil activity or ntds file creation found in any dataset.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No LSA Secrets (SECURITY\Policy\Secrets) access or lsadump/reg save activity found.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes were performed by lsass.exe itself, normal cached-credential maintenance.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No DCSync/drsuapi/lsadump command lines or replication activity found in sysmon or powershell.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity is the legitimate Azure Network Watcher agent (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe -> netsh trace start capture=yes) and Azure Guest Agent logman ETW traces on scranton.dmevals.local, both running as SYSTEM from Azure platform paths. No sniffing tools (tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap/dumpcap/tshark/pktmon), no npcap/winpcap/pcap driver loads, and no promiscuous/raw-socket command lines were found. No adversary network sniffing observed.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened LSASS with full access (0x1f3fff/0x1fffff) and pbeesly ran Get-PrivateKeys/Get-Clipboard/Invoke-ScreenCapture — credential and input capture on the host.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: pbeesly executed Get-Keystrokes (with a preceding Keystroke-Check AV-enumeration function) on scranton.dmevals.local — a PowerShell keylogger.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: pbeesly defined and invoked Invoke-ScreenCapture using System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing to capture the screen on scranton.dmevals.local.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: No web-portal capture artifacts: zero hits for IIS/wwwroot/inetpub/login file or process activity, and no HTTP POST in the zeek window.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: wsmprovhost.exe (remote PowerShell) opened LSASS with 0x1f3fff on nashua via a PowerShell Management cmdlet call trace, but no hooking DLL or explicit API-hook artifact was observed.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625 failed-logon events in windows.security; no brute-force authentication pattern. Credential access present on scranton is LSASS memory access (0x1FFFFF) and cert export, not brute force.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: No 4625 events and no password-iterating scripts; PowerShell Password/Credential hits are benign cert-export and 7-Zip archive password usage.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No SAM/SECURITY hive reads, no wordlist/potfile creation, no hash/crack tooling. LSASS handle opens are the credential-access mechanism, not offline cracking.

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No 4625 events, so no spray pattern. 4648 explicit-credential logons reflect pbeesly credential reuse via PSEXESVC for lateral movement, not spraying.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No 4625 events and no password-bearing command lines; no stuffing list or multi-account authentication attempts observed.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/token/smart-card interception artifacts in any dataset. All 'Credential' hits are benign Windows internals (Credential Guard disabled config, CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service registration, lsass DeviceGuard registry write). 4648 explicit-credential logons are PsExec (PSEXESVC.exe) and normal logon processes; LSASS access is svchost/powershell with GrantedAccess 0x1000. The only malicious artifact (Invoke-Exfil PowerShell using hardcoded creds for WebDAV exfil) is credential use/exfiltration, not MFA interception.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: Host 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local) attempted SMB to 192.168.0.4 on 445/139 (all REJ), then fell back to WebDAV over HTTP port 80 using the DavClnt and Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362 user agents, issuing OPTIONS/PROPFIND/PUT/LOCK/HEAD against /webdav and /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z with 401 challenges and successful PUT (201/204). This SMB-reject-then-WebDAV-redirector sequence is the canonical T1187 forced-authentication coercion chain to leak NTLM credentials.

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: On nashua.dmevals.local, wsmprovhost.exe (PowerShell remoting host) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff via PowerShell's Management module at 03:09:29, the only non-system/non-AV LSASS access in the dataset. It followed attacker PowerShell remoting (Invoke-Command -ComputerName NASHUA) and PsExec lateral movement with cleartext credentials from scranton, and the same session collected credential-named files (*pass*, *login*, *admin*, *vpn) and archived them. Consistent with exploitation/abuse of the remoting channel for credential access.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: All cookie-related hits are benign: WebDAV client DavSetCookie (davclnt.dll) process creations on scranton.dmevals.local and a WARP JIT service-package INetCookies file created by svchost.exe. No browser cookie database (Chrome/Edge/Firefox Cookies, Login Data, WebCache) was created or accessed, no cookie-stealing tooling or script was found, and process-access to browser/lsass processes used only routine access masks from svchost/Explorer. The credential and exfiltration activity present (plaintext PsExec creds, Invoke-Exfil 7-Zip to WebDAV, sdelete cleanup) is not web session cookie theft.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: accesschk.exe wrote a file named passwordsDB in C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite on scranton.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: pspasswd.exe/pspasswd64.exe staged in Downloads\SysinternalsSuite and hardcoded cleartext credentials (cozy/MyCozyPassw0rd!) embedded in the Invoke-Exfil script on scranton.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All Password/Credential registry value sets are legitimate OS activity by svchost/lsass/services/winlogon; no adversary credential storage.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No consolehost_history or shell-history file access found in sysmon or security data.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine certificate private keys to .pfx using hardcoded password 'saribas' on scranton.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: GptTmpl.inf reads from the Default Domain Policy GUID are normal Group Policy processing by machine accounts; no Groups.xml/cpassword access.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: pbeesly's PowerShell on SCRANTON opened LSASS with AccessMask 0x1FFFFF (full access) and ran Get-PrivateKeys exporting all machine certificate private keys to .pfx files with hardcoded password 'saribas'; staged via Invoke-Exfil to a WebDAV share.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: All browser credential-store checks (Login Data, logins.json, browser process/file access) returned zero hits across sysmon, security, powershell and other datasets.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: wsmprovhost.exe as pbeesly opened LSASS with 0x1f3fff on NASHUA (read/write process memory) shortly after the SCRANTON LSASS full-access event; LSASS memory access is the mechanism for harvesting Credential Manager/DPAPI secrets, but no explicit vault/DPAPI object access was logged.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: All password-manager checks (keepass/1password/bitwarden/lastpass/kdbx) returned zero hits across all four datasets.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: LSASS was accessed with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS (0x1fffff) by PowerShell on scranton, but this is credential theft (T1003), not modification of the authentication process. No authentication-process components were altered.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: LogonType 3 traffic is machine-account/DC authentication; 4648 events are PsExec lateral movement and routine winlogon logons. No DC authentication backdoor.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No password filter DLL dropped into System32 and no Notification Packages registry change (0 hits).

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: No 4739 policy change and no reversible-encryption configuration commands (0 hits).

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739/5136/4738 events and no MFA policy modification commands (0 hits).

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: No 5136 directory changes and no cloud/hybrid identity PowerShell cmdlets (0 hits).

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No NetworkProvider registry change and no network provider DLL installation (0 hits).

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: No AiTM positioning found: network-config commands (arp/route/netsh) were all spawned by legitimate Azure guest agents; DNS and SMB traffic is normal domain activity.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay: DNS queries resolved only legitimate names to the DC 10.0.0.4; 4697/7045 installs were PsExec/javamtsup (lateral movement), not relay; SMB was standard domain IPC$/SYSVOL access.

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: No ARP cache poisoning: the anomalous MACs are synthetic/placeholder (12:34:56:78:9a:bc) and randomized (fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1); arp.exe /a runs were Azure agent telemetry, not attacker reconnaissance.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP spoofing: no DHCP event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063) in windows.other, no DHCP ports 67/68 in Sysmon network connects, and no dhcp log type in the Zeek capture.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff during an active intrusion chain (malicious .scr -> cmd -> powershell stager), the credential-access step enabling Kerberos ticket theft.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: No golden-ticket artifacts: no krbtgt hash theft, no anomalous TGT forging, no golden/krbtgt references in PowerShell (C312 zero hits).

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: No silver-ticket artifacts: 4769 host-SPN requests are normal KDC-issued RC4 tickets with Failure Code 0x0; no silver/SPN forging scripts (C319 zero hits).

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL on newyork.dmevals.local requested TGS tickets for krbtgt and multiple machine accounts, all RC4 (0x12), consistent with Kerberoasting-style ticket harvesting.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: No AS-REP roasting indicators; no AS-REP/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth references in PowerShell (C334 zero hits).

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: Credential-access activity (LSASS access 0x1FFFFF by PowerShell, hidden steganographic PowerShell loader, WebDAV exfiltration) was observed on scranton, but no artifact of forging web credentials (cookie/SAML/token minting) was found.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: Only cookie-related event is a benign svchost INetCookies service-profile file; the matching PowerShell script block is a benign Sysinternals readme.ps1. No cookie forging or session-token manipulation observed.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: Zero hits for SAML/Assertion/NotOnOrAfter in PowerShell, process command lines, or Zeek HTTP URLs. PowerShell 4104 hits are the benign xActiveDirectory DSC module; windows.other 5857/5858 are routine WMI RSOP operations.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: No MFA request generation activity found. windows.security contains zero 4625 failed logons and only one 4776 (pbeesly); no authentication-challenge flood. The sole hit (C355, windows.other) is routine WMI provider starts (5857) and RSOP DeleteInstance cleanup (5858). PowerShell 'authenticat' matches are a Microsoft module manifest; Sysmon 'push' matches are the legitimate PushToInstall/dmwappushservice services; Zeek shows no MFA/IdP traffic.

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys function that recursively enumerated cert:\LocalMachine and exported every certificate with a thumbprint via Export-PfxCertificate to randomly-named .pfx files in Downloads (password 'saribas'), confirmed by Sysmon file-create of C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx by powershell.exe (PID 3876). A follow-up Invoke-BeachCleanup function deleted the .pfx/.bmp/.png artifacts. This is theft of authentication certificates/private keys (T1649).

checks.purpose: Stack all process creations to spot credential-dumping tools (mimikatz, procdump, comsvcs.dll rundll32) among rare executables.
Stack process-access targets to find LSASS or other credential-store processes being opened.
Stack object types accessed under handle/object-access auditing to find SAM/SECURITY/LSASS objects.
Stack newly created processes to spot dumping utilities launched on hosts.

args.query: event.code:4104 AND (powershell.script_block_text:*lsass* OR powershell.script_block_text:*mimikatz* OR powershell.script_block_text:*sekurlsa* OR powershell.script_block_text:*DumpCreds*)

checks.purpose: Find PowerShell script blocks referencing LSASS/credential-dumping APIs.
Look for credential-dumping references in other Windows event channels (service installs, VSS, etc.).
Stack granted-access masks on LSASS process opens to reveal memory-read access typical of dumping.
Read individual LSASS access events with source image and granted access.

args.query: FROM logs-windows.sysmon-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code == "10" AND (TO_LOWER(win.TargetImage) LIKE "*chrome.exe" OR TO_LOWER(win.TargetImage) LIKE "*firefox.exe" OR TO_LOWER(win.TargetImage) LIKE "*msedge.exe" OR TO_LOWER(win.TargetImage) LIKE "*iexplore.exe") | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, win.SourceImage, win.TargetImage, win.GrantedAccess, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Process-access events (Sysmon 10) against browser processes indicate memory-based browser credential theft.

args.query: FROM logs-windows.security-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code IN ("4663","4656","4658") AND (TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*login data*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*logins.json*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*key3.db*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*key4.db*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*google*chrome*user data*" OR TO_LOWER(win.ObjectName) LIKE "*mozilla*firefox*profiles*") | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, win.ObjectName, win.ProcessName, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Object-access auditing on browser credential-store files shows a process reading them.

args.query: FROM logs-windows.powershell-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE event.code IN ("4103","4104") AND (TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*login data*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*logins.json*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*key3.db*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*key4.db*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*sharpchrome*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(powershell.script_block_text, win.ScriptBlockText, "")) LIKE "*lazagne*") | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, user.name, powershell.script_block_text, _id, _index

checks.purpose: PowerShell scripts targeting browser credential stores or running browser-credential extraction modules.

args.query: FROM logs-windows.other-default METADATA _id, _index | WHERE TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*login data*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*logins.json*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*chrome*" OR TO_LOWER(COALESCE(message, win.Message, "")) LIKE "*firefox*" | KEEP @timestamp, host.name, event.code, message, _id, _index

checks.purpose: Other Windows channels may log browser credential-store file access or browser-related activity.
Detect processes opening handles to lsass.exe, which is how Credential Manager secrets (DPAPI vaults) are commonly harvested.

findings.title: PowerShell.exe opened LSASS with PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS on scranton
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, SourceProcessGUID {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS) and 0x1F3FFF within the same second. This is the access mask required to read LSASS memory for credential dumping and is not normal for PowerShell. It occurs in the same session/user context (pbeesly) that ran the Invoke-Exfil PowerShell script on this host, indicating an adversary dumping credentials.

findings.title: PowerShell full-access handle to LSASS and private-key/clipboard capture on scranton
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16 UTC on scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, entity {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and then 0x1FFFFF — full process access consistent with reading credential memory. In the same session user pbeesly ran 'Get-PrivateKeys' (dumping certificate private keys to .pfx files using a hardcoded password 'saribas'), 'Get-Clipboard', and 'Invoke-ScreenCapture'. Together these are input/credential capture actions on the host.

findings.title: PowerShell Get-Keystrokes keylogger executed by pbeesly on scranton
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:06:59 UTC on scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed the PowerShell command 'Get-Keystrokes;Start-Sleep -Seconds 15;View-Job -JobName "Keystrokes"' (PowerShell script-block logging event 4104, ScriptBlockId 7c8ce66d-dd1a-4a72-8e88-42dd7ff48c74). Immediately before, at 03:06:47, the same user defined a 'Keystroke-Check' function that enumerates known antivirus processes (avp, acs, outpost, mcvsescn, mcods, navapsvc, kav, AvastSvc, AvastUi, nod32krn, nod32, ekern, dwengine, MsMpEng, msseces, ekrn, savservice, scfservice, savadminservice) — a hallmark anti-AV check of the Get-Keystrokes keylogger tool. The job was later viewed (03:07:36) and removed (03:07:49). This is a keylogger capturing keystrokes on the host.

findings.title: Invoke-ScreenCapture GUI capture function executed by pbeesly on scranton
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:53 UTC on scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly defined and invoked an 'Invoke-ScreenCapture' function that uses System.Windows.Forms.SystemInformation::VirtualScreen and System.Drawing to repeatedly capture the screen to .bmp files in the user's Downloads folder, then ran 'Invoke-ScreenCapture;Start-Sleep -Seconds 3;View-Job -JobName "Screenshot"'. This is GUI/screen input capture on the host.

findings.title: PowerShell Invoke-Exfil script uses hardcoded credentials for WebDAV exfiltration (not MFA interception)
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly executed a PowerShell script block (event 4104) defining function Invoke-Exfil that compresses the user's Downloads folder with 7Zip4Powershell and exfiltrates it to a WebDAV share at \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials (username 'cozy', password 'MyCozyPassw0rd!'). This is credential use and data exfiltration, not MFA interception, so it does not substantiate T1111; it is reported here as the only genuinely malicious artifact surfaced by the T1111 hunt.

findings.title: WebDAV forced-authentication coercion from scranton (10.0.1.4) to 192.168.0.4
findings.summary: Host 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local) attempted SMB to 192.168.0.4 on ports 445 and 139, all of which were rejected (zeek.conn_state REJ), then immediately fell back to WebDAV over HTTP port 80. The first probe used the 'DavClnt' user agent (OPTIONS / -> 403), followed by a sustained series of 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362' requests (OPTIONS, PROPFIND, PUT, LOCK, HEAD) against /webdav and /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z, many answered 401 Unauthorized before succeeding (PUT 201/204, LOCK 200, HEAD 200, PROPFIND 207). This SMB-reject-then-WebDAV-fallback sequence with the Windows WebDAV redirector user agent is the classic T1187 forced-authentication pattern used to coerce a victim host into authenticating to an attacker-controlled WebDAV/SMB listener and leak NTLM credentials. All 36 WebDAV method requests in the dataset originate solely from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4.

findings.title: PowerShell remoting host (wsmprovhost.exe) opened LSASS with full access on NASHUA during attacker session
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:09:29.430Z, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, the WinRM/PowerShell-remoting host) opened C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff (full access). The call trace runs through PowerShell's Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, i.e. the access was driven by a PowerShell command executed in the remoting session, not by an OS component. This is the only non-system/non-AV process to touch LSASS in the dataset. The only credential reuse is pbeesly's own valid credentials used via PsExec/4648 for lateral movement, which is not credential stuffing.

findings.title: No MFA interception activity; 'Credential' hits are benign Windows internals
findings.summary: Hunting for T1111 (Multi-Factor Authentication Interception) across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.powershell and windows.other produced no evidence of MFA/token/smart-card interception. All 'Credential'-related hits are standard Windows components: Wininit event 14 logging 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' (Credential Guard disabled) on scranton, lsass.exe setting HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled to 0x00000000 at boot, and services.exe registering the built-in CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc service. Explicit-credential logons (4648) are dominated by user pbeesly via C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe (PsExec) and normal winlogon/svchost/taskhostw processes. LSASS handle access (Sysmon 10) is almost entirely svchost.exe/powershell.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION), consistent with benign security tooling. No MFA provider, OTP, smart-card or token-interception artifacts were observed.

findings.title: Routine LSASS handle accesses by system/AV/telemetry processes are benign
findings.summary: The bulk of Sysmon event 10 hits targeting lsass.exe come from legitimate components: svchost.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 (query-limited), Microsoft Azure IaaSAntimalware AntimalwareConfig.exe and WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe with 0x1400/0x1000, and wininit.exe/csrss.exe with 0x1fffff at boot. These are normal OS/security-product behaviours and are not exploitation for credential access.

findings.title: WebDAV DavSetCookie process creation is benign WebDAV client cookie handling
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly, rundll32.exe was spawned by svchost.exe with command line 'rundll32.exe C:\windows\system32\davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav' (5 occurrences, 2020-05-01 23:08:50 to 23:10:23). This is the standard Windows WebDAV client (davclnt.dll) setting a WebDAV cookie for the mapped http://192.168.0.4/webdav share, not theft of a browser session cookie. The same command line appears in Sysmon process-creation events on the same host.

findings.title: INetCookies file creation by svchost is a WARP JIT service package artifact
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, svchost.exe (PID 7200, SYSTEM) created C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-b484-4973-bbf2-a04208ecd4d4\AC\INetCookies at 2020-05-02T03:21:05.681Z. This is a per-package WinINet cookie store under the LocalService service profile for the Windows WARP JIT package, created by a system service, not a browser session cookie being stolen. No browser cookie database (Chrome/Edge/Firefox Cookies, Login Data, WebCache) was created or accessed anywhere in the dataset.

findings.title: No browser cookie-store access or cookie-stealing tooling observed
findings.summary: Across windows.sysmon, windows.security, windows.powershell and windows.other, the only 'cookie'-related artifacts are the benign WebDAV DavSetCookie and the WARP JIT INetCookies file. Sysmon process-access (event 10) to browser processes (MicrosoftEdge.exe, MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe, MicrosoftEdgeSH.exe) and lsass.exe came only from svchost.exe and Explorer.EXE with routine access masks (0x1000, 0x2000, 0x3000), consistent with normal system operation rather than memory scraping for session cookies. No PowerShell script block, process command line, or file creation referenced browser cookie databases or cookie-theft utilities.

findings.title: Explicit-credential logons (4648) by pbeesly to NASHUA via PsExec
findings.summary: 15 event.code 4648 explicit-credential logons were observed. pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local used explicit credentials targeting server NASHUA, and on nashua.dmevals.local C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe performed 4648 logons as pbeesly to localhost. The remaining 4648s are routine winlogon/taskhostw DWM/UMFD/machine-account logons. This reflects PsExec-based lateral movement using pbeesly's own credentials, not credentials harvested from files; no file-based credential source was observed.

findings.title: Registry Password/Credential value sets are OS-internal, not credential storage
findings.summary: 17 Sysmon event.code 13 registry value sets matched Password/Credential paths. All are legitimate OS activity: svchost.exe setting HKU\.DEFAULT\Software\Microsoft\IdentityCRL\ProviderPasswordLength/CharacterGroups on nashua and scranton, lsass.exe setting DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled, services.exe registering CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc, and winlogon.exe setting Winlogon\PasswordExpiryNotification. No adversary-written credential values were found.

findings.title: No shell-history credential access observed
findings.summary: No events referencing consolehost_history or PowerShell history files were found in windows.sysmon process-creation or windows.security file-access data. No shell-history credential collection was observed.

findings.title: SMB reads of GptTmpl.inf from Default Domain Policy by machine accounts
findings.summary: Zeek smb_files records show hosts 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 opening \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\sysvol paths including dmevals.local\Policies\{31B2F340-016D-11D2-945F-00C04FB984F9}\Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT\SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf. Windows security 5145 events on newyork.dmevals.local show the same GptTmpl.inf read by machine accounts SCRANTON$ and NASHUA$. This is the standard Default Domain Policy GUID being read during normal Group Policy processing by computer accounts, not GPP cpassword harvesting (no Groups.xml/cpassword access observed).

The majority of LSASS process-access events are routine: svchost.exe, services.exe, csrss.exe, wininit.exe, taskhostw.exe, RuntimeBroker.exe, backgroundTaskHost.exe, dsregcmd.exe, sppsvc.exe, wmiprvse.exe and Windows Defender MsMpEng.exe opening lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000/0x1400/0x1478/0x1fffff as part of normal OS operation. Also benign is lsass.exe itself opening C:\Windows\Temp\sdelete64.exe (0x1478) — the reverse direction, part of SDelete's normal operation. The WindowsAzure CollectGuestLogs.exe reading lsass.exe (0x1410) on all four hosts is Azure guest-log collection. These are not credential theft.
findings.title: Benign LSASS handle accesses by system processes
Network logons are machine-account/DC replication traffic, no DC authentication backdoor
findings.summary: The 218 LogonType 3 (network) 4624 events are dominated by the machine account NEWYORK$ logging on to newyork.dmevals.local from ::1, fe80:: and 10.0.0.4 — normal computer-account/DC authentication traffic. The 15 explicit-credential 4648 events are pbeesly authenticating to NASHUA via PSEXESVC.exe (lateral movement) and routine winlogon DWM/UMFD localhost logons. No evidence of a domain-controller authentication backdoor (no Skeleton Key / DSRM / authentication-package tampering).

findings.title: No password filter DLL registered or dropped
findings.summary: No file creation of a DLL into System32 matching cryptdll/msv1_0/samlib/passwordfilter/networkprovider (0 hits), no 4657 registry change to Notification Packages or Password keys (0 hits), and no 4688/4104 referencing Notification/PasswordFilter (0 hits). No password filter DLL was installed.

findings.title: No reversible-encryption setting enabled
findings.summary: Event 4739 (domain policy change) returned 0 hits, and no 4688/4104/sysmon process command line referenced Reversible/AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption/Set-ADUser/dsmod. No account was configured to store a reversibly-encrypted password.

findings.title: No MFA configuration tampering
findings.summary: No 4739/5136/4738 events (0 hits) and no Set-ADUser/Set-ADAuthenticationPolicy command lines. The only Authentication-related registry writes are routine LogonUI/FaceLogon session state written by LogonUI.exe and RuntimeBroker.exe, not MFA policy changes.

findings.title: No hybrid-identity / cloud-auth modification
findings.summary: No 5136 directory-service changes (0 hits) and no Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD/Set-AzureAD* PowerShell (0 hits). The dsregcmd.exe image load of cryptdll.dll on newyork is a normal device-registration operation, not hybrid-identity tampering.

findings.title: No network provider DLL registered
findings.summary: No 4657 registry change to NetworkProvider/Credential keys (0 hits) and no PowerShell referencing NetworkProvider/New-Item for a provider DLL (0 hits). No rogue network provider DLL was installed to capture credentials.

findings.title: No adversary-in-the-middle activity observed; network/name-resolution events are benign Azure agent and domain traffic
findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon, windows.other and zeek there is no evidence of an adversary positioning in the middle of network traffic. The only network-configuration commands on the Windows hosts (arp.exe /a, route.exe print, netsh trace start/stop) were all spawned by legitimate Azure guest agents (WaAppAgent.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe, NetworkWatcherAgent.exe) on scranton.dmevals.local, i.e. routine Azure VM telemetry. DNS resolution (Sysmon 22) resolved only legitimate names to the domain controller 10.0.0.4 and Microsoft endpoints. SMB/RPC activity (5140/5145) was standard machine-account access to IPC$/SYSVOL (lsarpc/samr) between domain hosts. No relay, poisoning or interception tooling was found.

findings.title: No name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay; DNS and SMB activity is normal domain traffic
findings.summary: Sysmon DNS query events (event.code 22) on scranton/newyork/nashua resolved only legitimate names: the domain controller NEWYORK.dmevals.local -> 10.0.0.4, localhost, wec.dmevals.local -> 10.0.1.10, and Microsoft telemetry endpoints. No LLMNR/NBT-NS-style lookups or responses from unauthorized hosts were seen. The 4697/7045 service-install events were PsExec (PSEXESVC) and a 'Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service' (javamtsup.exe) — lateral movement/execution, not name-resolution poisoning or SMB relay. Zeek SMB activity (smb_mapping to \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\IPC$, kerberos cifs/NASHUA) is standard domain authentication. No relay tooling in PowerShell script blocks.

findings.title: No ARP cache poisoning; MAC anomalies are synthetic/placeholder values and arp.exe runs are Azure agent telemetry
findings.summary: Zeek conn records show source IP 10.0.1.4 with two different source MACs (00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and a responder MAC of 12:34:56:78:9a:bc. The 12:34:56:78:9a:bc address is a well-known synthetic/placeholder MAC used in Zeek test data, and fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 is a locally-administered/randomized MAC — neither indicates a single attacker MAC claiming multiple IPs. The only ARP-related commands on the Windows hosts were 'arp.exe /a' invocations, all spawned by legitimate Azure guest agents (WaAppAgent.exe, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe, WindowsAzureGuestAgent.exe) on scranton.dmevals.local, i.e. routine Azure VM telemetry rather than attacker ARP reconnaissance.

findings.title: No DHCP spoofing; no DHCP-related events or traffic observed
findings.summary: No DHCP spoofing indicators exist in the data. The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP-related event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063) — the stacked event codes are unrelated (5858/5857/7045/7040 etc.). Sysmon network-connect destination ports (event.code 3) show no DHCP traffic (no ports 67/68); the observed ports are normal (8443, 389, 88, 53, 135, 445, 443). The Zeek capture contains no dhcp log type (only conn/files/ssl/x509/dce_rpc/http/dns/kerberos/smb_*). The Dhcp client service (svchost -s Dhcp) start on scranton is a normal service start.

findings.title: No golden-ticket indicators observed
findings.summary: No evidence of golden-ticket forging was found. All 28 Kerberos service-ticket requests (4769) used TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (RC4) with normal TicketOptions; there were no 4768/4769 anomalies, no krbtgt hash theft artifacts, and no PowerShell script blocks referencing golden/krbtgt (C312 zero hits). The krbtgt TGS requests seen are ordinary service-ticket requests, not forged TGTs.

findings.title: No silver-ticket indicators observed
findings.summary: No evidence of silver-ticket forging. The 4769 service-ticket requests for host SPNs (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) all carry normal TicketOptions and RC4 encryption and were issued by the KDC with Failure Code 0x0; no PowerShell script blocks referencing silver/service-ticket/SPN forging were found (C319 zero hits).

findings.title: No AS-REP roasting indicators observed
findings.summary: No evidence of AS-REP roasting. No PowerShell script blocks referencing AS-REP/asrep/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth were found (C334 zero hits), and no anomalous AS-REP request patterns were observed in the available data.

The only cookie-related file event is a svchost.exe creating C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_...\AC\INetCookies on scranton — a normal Windows service-profile INetCookies store, not browser cookie theft or forgery. The single PowerShell 4104 hit matching 'cookie/token/session' is a benign Sysinternals readme.ps1 helper (Get-AttributesMask) that merely documents SE_GROUP_LOGON_ID token attributes. No Set-Cookie manipulation, session-token forging, or browser cookie tampering was observed.

findings.title: No failed-logon or authentication-challenge burst in windows.security
findings.summary: Aggregating windows.security authentication events shows no 4625 (failed logon) events at all, and only a single 4776 credential-validation event (for pbeesly on newyork.dmevals.local). Successful logons (4624) are dominated by machine accounts (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$, UTICA$, WEC$) and SYSTEM, with pbeesly as the only interactive user. The 4648 explicit-credential events are routine (winlogon.exe for DWM/UMFD session accounts, taskhostw.exe, svchost.exe, and PSEXESVC.exe for pbeesly). This pattern is normal Windows authentication, not the repeated authentication-prompt flood characteristic of MFA request generation.

findings.title: PowerShell and Sysmon keyword hits are benign Windows components
findings.summary: The PowerShell 4104 hits matching 'authenticat' are a Microsoft module manifest (ModuleVersion 2.16.0.0, Author 'Microsoft Corporation') on newyork.dmevals.local, not MFA tooling. The Sysmon process-creation hits matching 'push' are the legitimate Windows services PushToInstall (svchost.exe -k netsvcs -p -s PushToInstall, started via sc.exe start pushtoinstall registration) and dmwappushservice on scranton.dmevals.local. Neither is an MFA push-notification generator. Zeek shows no MFA/identity-provider traffic (no okta/duo/mfa DNS queries or login/auth URLs); its 2140 events are conn/files/ssl/x509/dce_rpc/http/dns/kerberos/smb, with no authentication-prompt activity.

findings.title: SystemCertificates ROOT certificate blob modified on nashua (benign OS certificate store activity)
findings.summary: On nashua.dmevals.local a single registry value modification (event 4657) touched \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\ROOT\Certificates\BE36A4562FB2EE05DBB3D32323ADF445084ED656 (Blob), performed by account NASHUA$ (S-1-5-18, Logon ID 0x3E7) with process C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe. This is a single SYSTEM-context write to the machine ROOT certificate store, consistent with normal OS certificate-store maintenance rather than attacker certificate forging; no corresponding export/forging tooling was observed on nashua.

incidents.rationale: All describe the same action: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user pbeesly) opening lsass.exe (PID 736) on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16 with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF, the access mask used to read LSASS memory for credential dumping. incidents.title: Invoke-ScreenCapture GUI capture on scranton
incidents.rationale: pbeesly defined and invoked Invoke-ScreenCapture using System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing to write screen captures to the Downloads folder, i.e. GUI input capture.

incidents.title: WebDAV forced-authentication coercion from scranton to 192.168.0.4

incidents.rationale: Same source 10.0.1.4 accessed SYSVOL/IPC$/ADMIN$ on newyork and nashua as SCRANTON$ and pbeesly, consistent with credential-bearing SMB activity accompanying the WebDAV coercion, though such access is also common in legitimate administration.

incidents.title: accesschk.exe created a file named passwordsDB on scranton
incidents.rationale: accesschk.exe (PID 9204, launched by pbeesly) created C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB; the credential-themed name is suspicious but accesschk is a legitimate ACL tool and no credential content was observed. F28 and F62 describe the same file-creation event.

incidents.title: Sysinternals pspasswd credential tooling staged on scranton
incidents.rationale: pbeesly's PowerShell wrote pspasswd64.exe/pspasswd.exe into Downloads\SysinternalsSuite; staging credential-manipulation tooling is consistent with credential access via unsecured tooling.

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys exported machine certificates to .pfx on scranton
incidents.rationale: pbeesly ran Get-PrivateKeys, enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and exporting each certificate's private key to .pfx files protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas' — private-key theft. F27 and F64 describe the same script and export action.

incidents.title: Kerberos service-ticket requests for krbtgt and machine accounts by pbeesly (RC4)
incidents.rationale: pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL requested 4769 TGS tickets for machine accounts and krbtgt with RC4 encryption, consistent with Kerberoasting-style ticket requests.

incidents.title: Get-PrivateKeys certificate theft and Invoke-BeachCleanup anti-forensic cleanup
incidents.rationale: F58 covers the Get-PrivateKeys export of all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx (certificate theft); F59 covers Invoke-BeachCleanup deleting the exported .pfx and staging artifacts, the anti-forensic complement to the same certificate-theft action.

incidents.title: No password spraying; 4648 explicit-credential logons are PsExec lateral movement
incidents.rationale: No 4625 events exist, so no spray pattern; the 4648 explicit-credential logons show pbeesly credential reuse with PSEXESVC for lateral movement, not brute force.

incidents.title: PsExec with cleartext credentials to NASHUA before LSASS access
incidents.rationale: pbeesly repeatedly launched PsExec64.exe against \\NASHUA with the password in cleartext on the command line, i.e. lateral movement using valid credentials, not credential access.

incidents.title: Invoke-Exfil WebDAV exfiltration with hardcoded credentials (not MFA interception)
incidents.rationale: pbeesly's Invoke-Exfil compresses Downloads and exfiltrates to a WebDAV share using hardcoded credentials; this is credential use and exfiltration, not MFA interception.

incidents.title: Adjacent credential/exfil activity is not web session cookie theft
incidents.rationale: PsExec with plaintext credentials, Invoke-Exfil to WebDAV, and sdelete cleanup are credential use, exfiltration and anti-forensics, not theft of web session cookies.
